title: I Didn't Think I Would See Your Face — Adoption, Hands Laid On, a Double Portion
blocks: Brothers and sisters, peace be with you. Today there is a question I want to ask before anything else: when a person comes to the last stretch of his life, what is it that he remembers?
In Genesis chapter 48, Jacob is a hundred and forty-seven years old and lying on a sick bed. Joseph comes to see him, bringing his two sons with him, and the old man forces himself upright and sits.

And the first thing he opens his mouth to speak about is a night at Bethel more than seventy years earlier; the second thing is Rachel, who died on the road to Ephrath — he even remembers, in that much detail, that there was "still some distance to come."
And then he says the most moving sentence in the whole chapter: "I didn't think I would see your face, and behold, God has let me see your offspring also."
What he lost was one. What God gave back was three.
1. The Man Who Made Himself Sit Up
"After these things, someone said to Joseph, 'Behold, your father is sick.' He took with him his two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim." (Genesis 48:1)
"Sick" is חֹלֶה (*choleh*) — and this is the first time the word for falling ill appears anywhere in the Old Testament.
"Someone told Jacob, and said, 'Behold, your son Joseph comes to you,' and Israel strengthened himself, and sat on the bed." (Genesis 48:2)
"Strengthened himself" is וַיִּתְחַזֵּק (*vayyitchazzeq*), and it is a reflexive form — "he made himself strong." He propped himself up with his own strength.

Brothers and sisters, that picture is worth keeping. An old man of a hundred and forty-seven, ill in his bed, hears that his son and his grandsons have come — and he hauls himself upright and gets himself properly seated.
Because he has something he means to do. Blessing the next generation is something you sit up to do.
Then he opens his mouth, and his first sentence is this:
"God Almighty appeared to me at Luz in the land of Canaan, and blessed me." (Genesis 48:3)
"God Almighty" is אֵל שַׁדַּי (*El Shaddai*); and Luz is the old name of Bethel.
That was more than seventy years ago. He was a young man on the run at the time, sleeping out in open country with a stone under his head.

So much has happened in one lifetime: Laban changing his wages ten times over, the wrestling at Peniel, the bloodshed at Shechem, twenty-two years of mourning a son, and now seventeen quiet, comfortable years in Egypt.
And the first thing he wants to hand over as he dies is what God said to him on that one night.
Brothers and sisters, what will you speak of first at the end? Whatever that thing is, it is usually the thing you have actually believed all your life.
And then he does something very unusual:
"Now your two sons, who were born to you in the land of Egypt before I came to you into Egypt, are mine; Ephraim and Manasseh, even as Reuben and Simeon, will be mine." (Genesis 48:5)
"Are mine" is only two words in the Hebrew: לִי־הֵם (*li-hem*). It is the most compact declaration of adoption in the Old Testament.

And the example he reaches for is a striking one — "even as Reuben and Simeon." Those are the two disqualified elder brothers: one of them defiled his father's concubine, and the other butchered the city of Shechem.
What he means is this: these two boys weigh exactly as much in my heart as my own firstborn sons do.

And the consequence of that is extremely practical. When Israel later divided up the land, the tribe of Levi received no inheritance, because they were set apart to serve God; and Joseph's one tribe became two — Ephraim and Manasseh — which is precisely the share that was missing.
God's system has an arithmetic of its own. To establish God's system is to adopt the next generation in and count them as your own.

It works the same way in the church. If you look after only the few who are your own by birth, this household will never have more than one generation in it. Spiritual parents are the people who are willing to say, "These two are mine."
"Israel strengthened himself, and sat on the bed" — why is that one movement worth remembering?

The Hebrew is a reflexive form; literally, "he made himself strong." He propped himself up with his own strength. Here is an old man of a hundred and forty-seven, ill in his bed, who hears that his son and his grandsons have come and hauls himself upright to sit properly. Because he has something he means to do: blessing the next generation is something you sit up to do. And that picture is a reminder to everyone who is an elder or a leader — a blessing is not a line you toss out lying down; it is something you rouse yourself for and do formally. In practice it is very simple: put it in the diary. Choose a time and an occasion, and say your blessing over that child properly.
Why is the first thing he hands over as he dies a single night more than seventy years ago?

His opening sentence is, "God Almighty appeared to me at Luz in the land of Canaan, and blessed me." Luz is the old name of Bethel — that was the night he slept with a stone under his head while he was running for his life. So much had happened since: Laban changing his wages ten times over, the wrestling at Peniel, the bloodshed at Shechem, twenty-two years of mourning a son, seventeen comfortable years in Egypt. And the thing he speaks of first at the end is what God said on that one night. That gives us a very good self-examination: what will you speak of first at the end? Whatever that thing is, it is usually the thing you have actually believed all your life. You can put the question to yourself once today.
2. A Light from the Original: As for Me, Rachel Died Beside Me
What comes next, in verse 7, is very abrupt. Halfway through what he is saying, the old man suddenly turns a corner:

"As for me, when I came from Paddan, Rachel died beside me in the land of Canaan on the way, when there was still some distance to come to Ephrath, and I buried her there on the way to Ephrath (also called Bethlehem)." (Genesis 48:7)
Everything on either side of it is about the adoption. This verse looks as though it did not need to be here at all.
But brothers and sisters, this verse is the thing that has been sitting in that old man's heart for more than forty years.
"Died beside me" is מֵתָה עָלַי רָחֵל (*metah alai Rachel*), and that preposition עָלַי carries the sense of a weight pressing down — she died on me, she has lain on me ever since.

"When there was still some distance to come to Ephrath" — the Hebrew is כִּבְרַת־אֶרֶץ (*kivrat-eretz*), a rare expression that occurs only three times in the whole Old Testament, and every time it has to do with Rachel.
He remembers that road. He remembers how much further there still was to go. Forty years and more, and he remembers it still.
Some wounds stay for a lifetime.

Scripture does not delete this verse, and it does not add a line saying, "but by then he had made his peace with it." It simply lets the old man, in the middle of giving a blessing, say one sentence about his pain.

And now we understand why he says it at this particular moment: he is on the point of counting Joseph's two sons as his own sons — and Joseph is Rachel's son. What he is thinking is: these are what she left behind.
He also mentions, almost in passing, that it happened at Bethlehem. The text goes out of its way to add that footnote.
A mother buried by the side of a road at Bethlehem; and seventeen hundred years later, another mother gave birth to a baby in that same small town. God remembers every grave on every road.
Then verse 8: "Israel saw Joseph's sons, and said, 'Who are these?'"
It is not that he fails to recognise them — this is the question of acknowledgement inside an adoption ceremony, rather like the minister at a wedding today asking, "Who is this?"
Joseph answers, "They are my sons, whom God has given me here." — and "here" means in Egypt. The sons he was given in the place of his suffering are now counted into the family of the covenant.

"Now the eyes of Israel were dim for age, so that he couldn't see well." — the Hebrew is literally "the eyes of Israel were heavy from old age", כָּבְדוּ מִזֹּקֶן, and it is almost exactly the situation of Isaac back in chapter 27.
Back then it was he who took advantage of a father's failing eyes in order to steal a blessing. Now it is his turn to have failing eyes — and he is the one giving the blessing away.
"Joseph brought them near to him; and he kissed them, and embraced them."
"Embraced" is וַיְחַבֵּק (*vayechabbeq*), an intensive form — he held them tightly.
"Israel said to Joseph, 'I didn't think I would see your face, and behold, God has let me see your offspring also.'" (Genesis 48:11)
"I didn't think" is לֹא פִלָּלְתִּי (*lo fillalti*), and the root of that word is the same root as the word for "to pray" — "I did not dare so much as to think it, let alone to ask for it."
Brothers and sisters, this is the tenderest verse in the chapter.
What he did not dare ask for, God gave him. And not one, but three — a son, and two grandsons on top of him.
What God gives us is very often more than we dare open our mouths and ask for.
He is halfway through, and suddenly he brings up Rachel's death. Has that verse wandered off the point?

It has not. That is the thing that has been sitting in the old man's heart for more than forty years. The preposition behind "died beside me" carries the sense of a weight pressing down — she died on him, she has lain on him ever since; and "when there was still some distance to come to Ephrath" uses a rare expression that occurs only three times in the whole Old Testament, and every time it has to do with Rachel. He remembers that road. He remembers how much further there still was to go. Forty years and more, and he remembers it still. Some wounds stay for a lifetime. And Scripture does not delete the verse, and it does not add a line saying, "but by then he had made his peace with it" — it simply lets the old man, in the middle of giving a blessing, say one sentence about his pain.
"I didn't think I would see your face" — why is that sentence so tender?

The root of the Hebrew behind "I didn't think" is the same root as the word for "to pray"; it means "I did not dare so much as to think it, let alone to ask for it." What he lost was one; what God gave back was three — a son, and two grandsons on top of him. What God gives us is very often more than we dare open our mouths and ask for. And this verse carries a very practical reminder as well: the thing you do not dare ask for, you may ask for; and the thing you asked for and did not get does not mean that God has given you any less. Here is a practice you can do. List three things in your life that you never dared imagine and that happened anyway. You will find that you have been keeping your accounts far too conservatively.
What comes next is the most famous picture in the chapter.

Joseph arranges the two boys with great care: Ephraim in his own right hand, facing his father's left hand; Manasseh in his own left hand, facing his father's right hand. The firstborn on the right, the younger on the left. There is no possible way to get it wrong.

"Israel stretched out his right hand, and laid it on Ephraim's head, who was the younger, and his left hand on Manasseh's head, guiding his hands knowingly, for Manasseh was the firstborn." (Genesis 48:14)
"Guiding his hands" is שִׂכֵּל אֶת־יָדָיו (*sikkel et-yadav*). The root of that verb means to act prudently, to do a thing with insight.
Which is to say: the text uses a verb meaning "wisely" in order to describe this crossing of the arms.
Joseph saw it and was displeased, and tried to move his father's hand back across: "Not so, my father, for this is the firstborn. Put your right hand on his head."
And his father said two words, and he said them twice:
Brothers and sisters, this is not an old man losing his grip. This is deliberate.

And think for a moment about who it is who is saying it. He is the younger brother himself — he is the second son who was born gripping his brother's heel and who later got hold of the birthright. Nobody on earth knows better than he does what that birthright cost him over a lifetime.

Isaac was not the firstborn. Jacob was not the firstborn. Perez was not the one who put out his hand first. Ephraim was not the firstborn. This is a line that runs all the way through Genesis: God's choosing does not follow the human order.

Why not? Paul says it most clearly of all in 1 Corinthians: "God chose the lowly things of the world, and the things that are despised, and the things that don't exist, that he might bring to nothing the things that exist, that no flesh should boast before God."

And I want to say something here in particular, so that this is not misused: this principle does not say that the firstborn does not matter, or that our elders do not matter. The point of the text is that no flesh should boast before God. It is not the belittling of anybody's place.

If you are the eldest son or the eldest daughter in your family, this chapter is not a denial of you. It is telling every one of us the same thing: your place is something God gives; it is not something you line up for.
And the content of the blessing is where this passage truly reaches its summit:
"The God before whom my fathers Abraham and Isaac walked, the God who has fed me all my life long to this day, the angel who has redeemed me from all evil, bless the lads." (Genesis 48:15–16)
The first: "the God before whom my fathers Abraham and Isaac walked" — he joins himself onto that line before he says anything else. Faith has a source.

The second: "the God who has fed me all my life long to this day." The Hebrew is הָרֹעֶה אֹתִי (*haro'eh oti*), "the One who has shepherded me" — and this is the first time in the whole Bible that anybody calls God his shepherd. The first voice of Psalm 23, "Yahweh is my shepherd", comes out of the mouth of a hundred-and-forty-seven-year-old shepherd.
He kept sheep all his life. He knows what shepherding is — daily, unglamorous, unbroken looking after. And he says: this is how God has dealt with me, all my life long, right up to today.

The third: "the angel who has redeemed me from all evil." "Redeemed" is גָּאַל (*ga'al*), the Old Testament's kinsman-redeemer — the near relative whose duty it is to buy back a relative's property and a relative's life.
A man who owned in his own words that "the days of the years of my life have been few and evil" says, at the end of his life: that One redeemed me the whole way, out of every trouble.
The bitterness was real. And so was the redemption.

And notice this: from beginning to end of that whole blessing, not once is an "I" the leading character. When he was young his mouth was full of "I" — I will have the blessing, I want the birthright, I take hold with all five fingers. At the end, his mouth is full of God.
There is the definition of maturity: when you are young your mouth is full of "I"; by the end, your mouth is full of "God."
Was the crossing of the hands an old man losing his grip?

It was not. The root of that verb means to act prudently, to do a thing with insight — the text uses a verb meaning "wisely" to describe the crossing of the arms. And when Joseph tried to move the hand back, he said, "I know, my son, I know." It was deliberate. What is even more worth pondering is who it is who is saying it: he is himself the second son who was born gripping his brother's heel and who later got hold of the birthright, and nobody on earth knows better than he does what that birthright cost him over a lifetime. Isaac was not the firstborn. Jacob was not the firstborn. Perez was not the one who put out his hand first — God's choosing does not follow the human order.
I want to ask you to look once more at that pair of crossed hands.

These are the hands that were born gripping a brother's heel; the hands that carried in the savoury dish and put on goatskins to deceive a father; the hands that rolled the great stone off the mouth of the well for Rachel; the hands that took hold of that man at Peniel and would not let go; the hands that received a bloodied coat and recognised it as their son's.
And now those hands are open, and crossed, and laid on the heads of two grandsons.
From grasping to letting go; from snatching a blessing to giving a blessing. That is the journey of Jacob's life, and it is the journey of every person who comes to believe.
At the last he says to Joseph, "Behold, I am dying, but God will be with you, and bring you again to the land of your fathers." (Genesis 48:21)
"I am dying, but God will be with you." — that is the last sentence every spiritual elder ought to leave behind him. Not "here is how much I am leaving you", but "God will be with you."
And then he says, "Moreover I have given to you one portion above your brothers, which I took out of the hand of the Amorite with my sword and with my bow."
"One portion" is שְׁכֶם אֶחָד (*shechem echad*), literally "one Shechem", and it can equally well be rendered "one shoulder." It is a play on words — Joseph would in the end be buried at Shechem.
The last chapter of Joshua records it: "They buried the bones of Joseph, which the children of Israel brought up out of Egypt, in Shechem."
One sentence, spoken by an old man on a sick bed, and honoured four hundred years later.
Does this line about God choosing the younger end up belittling the firstborn?

It does not, and this has to be said clearly so that it is not misused. Paul puts it most plainly of all in 1 Corinthians: "God chose the lowly things of the world, and the things that are despised, and the things that don't exist … that no flesh should boast before God." The point is that nobody may boast; it is not the belittling of anybody's place. If you are the eldest son or the eldest daughter in your family, this chapter is not a denial of you — it is telling every one of us the same thing: your place is something God gives, not something you line up for. And in the same way, no parent may use this chapter to underwrite favouritism. What Jacob crossed was the hands of blessing; he was not casting one of the children aside.
5. Distortions You Must Be Able to Spot
There are several places in this chapter to handle with care.

The first distortion is to preach the crossed hands as Jacob getting it wrong — as though his eyes were too dim and he laid them on the wrong heads. In verse 19 he says it himself: "I know, my son, I know." It was deliberate. Preach it as a slip and you lose the consistent principle of God's choosing. The test is: does the congregation see a confused old man, or an elder who is obeying?

The second distortion is to take "God chooses the one who comes later" and reason from it that the firstborn, or the older generation, does not matter. The point is that no flesh may boast before God; it is not the belittling of anybody's place. Misused, this does real damage inside families. The test is: when the eldest child in the room has heard you out, does he feel he has just been written off?

The third distortion is to preach the blessing as a ritual you can operate. The content of verses 15 and 16 is God from beginning to end — it is a confession of faith, not an incantation. Preach it as a ritual and the congregation will start chasing gestures and forms instead of saying God out loud to the next generation.

The fourth distortion is to skip the verse where he brings up Rachel. Verse 7 breaks in without warning because it is what the old man has carried for more than forty years. Skip it and you lose that honesty — that some wounds stay for a lifetime. The person sitting there with a grief of long standing has to walk out feeling that he was understood.

The fifth distortion is to preach "God gives you more than you lost" as a formula for compensation — lose one and you will be repaid three. Joseph came back; Rachel did not. Scripture honestly writes the two things side by side. God's grace is real and the pain of the loss is real, and you may not use the first to cancel out the second.
6. Two Real Questions from a Chinese Setting

The first question: we very seldom open our mouths and bless the next generation. We give money, we give a flat, we give advice, we give a telling-off — the one thing we rarely do is lay a hand on a head and, in God's name, say a specific word of blessing out loud. There are people who have gone a whole lifetime without once hearing a parent say, "I am proud of you." Brothers and sisters, Jacob propped up a sick body and sat himself up in order to do this. This week, please bless one person younger than you: say what you see in him, and say what you are asking God to do for him. It can be your child, your grandchild, your student, your spiritual son or daughter. Open your mouth. Do not leave it until it is too late.

The second question: when we tell our own story, we usually tell it as an epic of struggle. "How hard I had it in those years." "How I got myself through it." "I built all of this with these two hands." And when we have finished, what the children have learned is that you have to rely on yourself. Jacob's version goes like this: "the God who has shepherded me all my life long to this day, the angel who has redeemed me from all evil." The same life, two ways of telling it — and what gets handed on to the next generation is completely different. This week, when you tell your story, say more about God and less about yourself.
7. Living 321 Out — From a Hand That Grasps to a Hand That Blesses
Brothers and sisters, let us tie this lesson back into the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal of 321.

Jesus is my role model. Jacob says, "the God who has shepherded me all my life long to this day"; and the Lord Jesus says, "I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep." My role model is this: the One who shepherded me all my life became the shepherd in person, and became the sheep in person. So I too am to shepherd people, and not merely to manage them.

The Bible is my standard. The standard is not "it is only fair if we go in order of age." The standard is that God chose the things that do not exist, so that no flesh should boast before him. Our common sense objects — exactly as Joseph reached out to move the hand back across; and the standard answers: I know, my son, I know.

The Holy Spirit is my guide. A blessing is not read off a script. Every sentence Jacob said was something his own life had verified. When you bless somebody, ask the Holy Spirit to let you see what is really there in that person, and then say it out loud. Rely on your intellect and lean on yourself and you will be full of worry — you will be afraid of saying the wrong thing; rely on the heart and lean on the Holy Spirit and you will be glad.

Let Jesus be King. "I know, my son, I know." He deliberately broke the human order and went with God's choosing. To let Jesus be King is to hand over even the sequence I take for granted and let him rearrange it — including who goes first, who gets more, and who takes over.

Let Jesus receive all the glory. In that blessing there is not one line that says "I am giving you this"; the whole of it is "bless the lads." A man who can still hand the glory over when he is old has been practising that all his life.

Establish God's system. "These two sons are mine, even as Reuben and Simeon." To establish God's system is to adopt the next generation in and count them as your own. A man who develops only the children of his own body leaves behind an estate; a man who is willing to adopt leaves behind tribes.
"These two sons are mine" — how much weight is there in that sentence?

In the Hebrew it is only two words, the most compact declaration of adoption in the Old Testament. And the example he reaches for is a striking one — "even as Reuben and Simeon", the two disqualified elder brothers. What he means is that these two boys weigh exactly as much in his heart as his own firstborn sons do. And it had very practical consequences later, when the land was divided: the tribe of Levi received no inheritance because they were set apart to serve, and Joseph's one tribe became two, which is precisely the share that was missing. It works the same way in the church — if you look after only the few who are your own by birth, this household will never have more than one generation in it. Spiritual parents are the people who are willing to say, "These two are mine."
8. Four Kinds of Heart, the Same Pair of Hands Laid On
We stand in front of that sick bed with four kinds of heart.

The proud heart says, "My life is something I fought for and won on my own." Jacob lived that way when he was young as well — he grabbed, he traded, he calculated. And at the end he does not mention a single achievement of his own. Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, and writing God's work up in our own accounts; humility is returning to our originally intended position as human beings and saying, "the God who has shepherded me all my life long to this day."

The fearful heart says, "I have nothing to leave my children." You have. You have in your hands a story that God has walked you through, and a pair of hands you can lay on a child's head. What Jacob left behind by way of property was not much; what he left was one sentence — and that sentence has travelled four thousand years.

The ashamed heart says, "Somebody like me is not fit to bless anyone." Jacob deceived his father, fought for the birthright, played favourites, kept silent when he should have spoken. And God made him the one who blessed the twelve tribes of Israel. You do not bless people because you are worthy; you bless people because there is grace in your hands.

The wounded heart says, "The one I lost is never coming back." Neither was Jacob's. At a hundred and forty-seven he still remembered how much further there had been to go along that road. Scripture did not rub it out for him. And yet the same old man also said, "I didn't think I would see your face." The loss is real and God's doubling is real; the two of them live in the same heart, and they do not cancel each other out.
Four kinds of heart, and the same pair of hands laid on. And that pair of hands is crossed — because God's arithmetic is not the same as ours.
9. This Week, a Few Things You Can Do
First, towards God. Pray to him once using this name: "the God who has shepherded me all my life long to this day." Say those two phrases — "all my life long" and "to this day" — slowly, out loud.
Second, towards yourself. Write down one thing you never expected and God gave you anyway, and give thanks for it once.
Third, towards people. Bless one person younger than you, and be specific — say what you see in him, and say what you are asking God to do for him. You may lay hands on him; you may write it down.
Fourth, towards daily living. This week, when you tell your story, say more about God and less about yourself. Especially when you are telling it to your children.
Fifth, towards the mission. Adopt one spiritual son or daughter, and hand on to him what you have. You do not have to wait until you feel qualified. Just begin.

Sixth, tell it in three sentences to one friend outside the church. First: there is a man in the Bible who spent a whole lifetime grasping, and who propped himself up to sit and bless his grandsons before he died. Second: what he said was, "the God who has shepherded me all my life long to this day." Third: I hope that the last sentence of my life will also be about him, and not about me.
Brothers and sisters, let us declare together before God:
I declare that these hands of mine, which have grasped for so long, will open out to bless people.
I declare that I will no longer limit God by my own order; his choosing is his own to make.
I declare that I will adopt the next generation in and count them as my own.
I declare that in the story of my life, the leading character is God, and not me.
What three confessions are hidden inside the blessing he gives?

The first: "the God before whom my fathers Abraham and Isaac walked" — he joins himself onto that line before anything else; faith has a source. The second: "the God who has shepherded me all my life long to this day" — the Hebrew is "the One who has shepherded me", and this is the first time in the whole Bible that anybody calls God his shepherd; the first voice of Psalm 23 comes out of the mouth of a hundred-and-forty-seven-year-old shepherd. The third: "the angel who has redeemed me from all evil" — "redeemed" is the Old Testament's kinsman-redeemer. The bitterness was real; so was the redemption. And in the whole passage not one "I" is the leading character — when he was young his mouth was full of I; at the end, his mouth is full of God.

An old man, ill in his bed, hauls himself upright and sits properly. The first thing he speaks of is God appearing to him more than seventy years ago; the second thing he speaks of is a wife he lost more than forty years ago; and then he stretches out his hands, crossed, and lays them on the heads of two grandsons.
He says: the God who has shepherded me all my life long to this day, the angel who has redeemed me from all evil — bless the lads.

So the focus is on Jesus, not on ourselves, not on other people, not on our circumstances. Not I, but Christ. Because the One who "has shepherded me all my life long" later said, "I am the good shepherd"; and the angel who "redeemed me from all evil" later became our kinsman-redeemer, and bought us back with his own blood. And his hands, too, were once stretched wide open on a piece of wood — and that was the greatest blessing this world has ever been given.

May God bless every one of us, that we would open the hands we have kept clenched; may we dare to open our mouths and bless the next generation, and dare, when we tell our own story, to give the leading part to God; and may the last sentence any of us ever says be, "the God who has shepherded me all my life long to this day." In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

Leader's note: the Three Transformations are one road running downward. The first drives the point of this lesson into the head, the second carries it from the head into the heart, the third carries it from the heart into the days of the week. If time runs short, cover fewer questions rather than skipping the third — without reaching the third transformation, this lesson stops at a mindset.

Priority markers: ★★★ = highest priority; if time is short, discuss at least this one in each transformation. ★★ = second priority. ★ = if time allows. The multiplication assignment marked [Must do] may not be dropped; it can be finished at home.
Transformation One | Internalise — until it becomes mindset (about 20 minutes)
Purpose: through discussion, to drive the point of this lesson into a clear mindset.
1. ★★★ When you are young your mouth is full of "I"; by the end, your mouth is full of "God." Whereabouts on that line are you standing right now?
2. ★★ "These two sons are mine" — spiritual parents are the people who are willing to adopt the next generation. Whom have you adopted?
3. ★ In the middle of giving a blessing he said one sentence about a pain forty years old. Some wounds stay for a lifetime: is that a comfort to you, or a weight?
4. ★★ Your place is something God gives; it is not something you line up for. How does that sentence comfort you, and how does it correct you?
Leader's reminder: the aim of this section is that people can say it, not that they answer beautifully. If someone is speaking in fragments, help him tidy it up; do not finish his sentence for him.
Transformation Two | Digest — until it becomes life (about 35 minutes · the heart of this lesson)
Purpose: through seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing, to digest the mindset until it becomes life.

5. ★★★ The manuscript named four kinds of heart — proud (my branch of the family is the legitimate one), fearful (I am afraid I will run out of time to bless anyone), ashamed (I have nothing worth handing on to the next generation), wounded (nobody has ever laid a hand on my head). Which are you most like? What experience made you that way?
6. ★★ Read aloud: "the God who has shepherded me all my life long to this day." Then tell the group: where does that sentence touch you?
7. ★★ Is there a road in your own heart where you still remember exactly how much further there was to go? Where is that thing still pressing on you now?
8. ★ Finish this in one sentence: "If today were my last day, the one thing I would most want to say is …"
9. ★★ This week, whom are you going to lay hands on and bless? Give the name, the time, and the first sentence you are going to say.

Leader's reminder: the questions in this section will touch bereavement and losses of long standing. Do not say, "that is all in the past now." If someone speaks of a wound that has not healed in many years, stay with him first, and follow up with him privately after the meeting.
Transformation Three | Transform — until it becomes daily living (about 25 minutes)
Purpose: through discussing concrete application, to transform life into daily living.
10. ★★ In your own home, who is the child or the younger relative that nobody has laid a hand on yet? Say what you are going to do about it.
11. ★ The same question in another setting: in your church or at your workplace, who is the person of the next generation you could adopt?
12. ★★★ The shepherding practice: this week, write down three concrete facts about how "God has shepherded me all my life long", and read them out to one person. Say now whom you will read them to.
13. ★★ The 920 practice: find your one "2" — your spiritual companion — and bless each other's children or spiritual children once. Say his name out loud here and now.

14. ★★★ [Must do] Multiplication assignment: this week, tell this lesson to one friend outside the church in three sentences. First: there is an old man of a hundred and forty-seven in the Bible who was too ill to get up, and who heard that his grandsons had come and hauled himself upright to sit. Second: he laid his hands crossed on the heads of the two boys and said that God had shepherded him all his life long to this day. Third: so what I have learned is that what a person leaves the next generation at the end is the One he believed in. Write down now who you are going to tell.

In pairs, tell each other two things: the child or younger person you are going to bless, and the thing you never dared ask for and have already received. Then pray for each other, asking the Lord that our mouths would be full of him at the end, and that we would still have a blessing in our hands to lay down.
